NMD predictor head-to-head comparison

Our deep-learning model vs NMDetective-B vs the NMDEP rule-tree baseline

2026-06-21

1. Purpose & approach

This report benchmarks our deep-learning NMD predictor against two published variant-level NMD prediction models — NMDetective-B (Lindeboom et al. 2019) and the NMDEP rule-tree baseline (Saadat & Fellay 2025) — on the same long-read-observed isoforms, using a common continuous gold standard.

Three design choices distinguish this from the original NMDetective / NMDEP performance evaluations:

  1. Common gold standard. All three models are scored against the mashr posterior-mean log₂ fold-change of each isoform under SMG1 inhibition (4-CT cross-cell-type estimate), not against the TCGA-derived NMD-efficacy estimates the rule-based models were originally trained on. This is a cross-dataset generalisation test: the rule-based models are applied to a domain different from their training domain.

  2. Features computed from our isoforms, not by canonical-transcript lookup. For every isoform, the four NMDetective-B features (in-last-exon, distance-to-start, exon-length-at-stop, within-50-nt of last EJ) are computed directly from the long-read-observed transcript structure. This eliminates the canonical-transcript limitation of variant-level models.

  3. Test-set evaluation. Because our model has training-set isoforms in the broader cohort, all reported metrics use only the chr1 / chr3 / chr5 / chr7 held-out test split — isoforms the deep-learning model never saw at training time. The rule-based models also see these isoforms for the first time, so the comparison is symmetric.

Full-rank NMDetective-A (the random-forest variant) and the full NMDEP deep-learning model were deferred from this comparison because their trained weights / inference code are not publicly available (see §6).

2. Cohort

Test-set head-to-head cohort: 561 isoforms from 293 unique genes.
Subclass Isoforms Genes
NMD+/PTC+ 255 255
NMD+/PTC- 30 30
Control 276 276
Total 561 293

The Control comparators are gene-matched to a subset of the NMD-susceptible comparators, which is why the unique-gene count (293) is below the per-subclass sum.

3. Per-isoform feature computation

For each cohort isoform we computed the four NMDetective-B input features from its long-read-observed transcript structure:

Feature Definition
in_last_exon Is the comparator stop codon in the last exon of the transcript?
distance_to_start_nt Transcript-coordinate distance from the start codon to the stop codon (nt).
exon_length_at_stop_nt Length of the exon containing the stop codon (nt).
within_50nt_of_last_ej Is the stop codon within 50 nt upstream of the last exon-exon junction (i.e., not a PTC by the 50-nt rule)?

The stop codon used per subclass:

  • NMD+/PTC+: the reference-AUG-projected stop codon (comp_stop_tx_pos from Isopair::traceReferenceAtg()), avoiding the SQANTI/TD2 PTC-avoidance bias (see CLAUDE.md).
  • NMD+/PTC−: same reference-AUG-projected stop.
  • Control: the natural stop from the comparator’s own GENCODE-annotated CDS, projected into transcript coordinates.

4. Scoring

Three models scored on each isoform:

4.1 NMDetective-B

The published 4-rule decision tree (Lindeboom et al. 2019, Fig. 1c), applied to our features with the original thresholds:

  • in last exon → escape (leaf score 0.00)
  • distance to start < 150 nt → escape (0.12)
  • exon length at stop > 407 nt → escape (0.41)
  • within 50 nt of last EJ → escape (0.20)
  • otherwise → trigger NMD (0.65)

4.2 NMDEP rule-tree baseline

Same 4-rule structure with the NMDEP-re-optimised thresholds from Table 3 of Saadat & Fellay 2025: 49 / 120 / 355 nt. Leaf scores inherited from NMDetective-B for comparability of magnitudes. Agreement with NMDetective-B’s binary calls is 98.9% — the small threshold deltas only shift a handful of borderline cases.

4.3 Our model

Per-isoform predicted NMD probability from the trained CNN + attention model (peter4244/NMD_orf_model_v5_4ct, best_model_atg500_stop500.pt), restricted to the chr1/3/5/7 held-out test split.

5.1 Pooled

All three models reach a similar pooled performance on the test set: Spearman ρ 0.76 (NMDetective-B), 0.77 (NMDEP rule baseline), 0.76 (our model). This pooled near-equality reflects the easy separation of NMD-susceptible isoforms from non-NMD Controls, which all three models capture.

5.2 Stratified by PTC subclass

Within a single PTC subclass — where the easy between-class separation is removed — the deep-learning model substantially outperforms both rule-based predictors:

  • NMD+/PTC+ (n = 255): our model Spearman 0.34, vs. 0.19 (NMDetective-B) and 0.22 (NMDEP rule baseline).

  • NMD+/PTC− (n = 30): our model Spearman 0.51, while both rule-based models are negatively correlated with the gold standard (-0.14). This is by construction: every PTC− isoform is a real NMD substrate (median gold log-FC ≈ 2.3) that lacks a premature stop detectable by the 50-nt-rule cascade, so the rule-based models assign them all low scores. The deep-learning model recovers these substrates because it does not depend on a discrete PTC call.

  • Control (n = 276): our model Spearman 0.23, vs. essentially zero for both rule-based models (0.01 and 0.01). The rule-based models cluster all Control scores near zero (matching the Controls’ true log-FC ≈ 0 by coincidence, not by discrimination), which yields a small MAE but near-zero rank correlation.

7. Take-aways

  1. Pooled performance is uninformative for this comparison. The pooled Spearman of ≈0.76–0.77 across all three models would suggest equivalent predictive power; the within-subclass breakdown shows this is driven entirely by the (easy) Controls-vs-NMD-substrate separation.

  2. Rule-based predictors fail on PTC-negative NMD substrates. Both rule cascades classify every NMD+/PTC− isoform as “escape NMD” despite their being real NMD substrates by the mashr gold standard. The resulting Spearman ≈ −0.14 is small in magnitude only because the rule scores cluster on a few discrete leaves; the sign is the meaningful result.

  3. The deep-learning model retains within-subclass discrimination across all three subclasses. This pattern is consistent with the model learning continuous sequence and structural signal beyond the categorical 50-nt rule.

  4. The NMDetective-B vs NMDEP rule-tree threshold difference is immaterial at the scale of this cohort (98.9% binary-call agreement). The two rule-based predictors are effectively a single baseline.

8. Deferred models

Two model variants were not scored in this comparison because their trained weights / inference code are not publicly available:

  • Full-rank NMDetective-A (Lindeboom 2019) — the random-forest variant. The associated figshare deposit (10.6084/m9.figshare.7803398) contains only precomputed per-nucleotide NMD scores as GTF files for canonical UCSC knownGene transcripts (hg19 / hg38 / mm9 / mm10), with no model object or inference code released.

  • Full NMDEP MLP (Saadat & Fellay 2025) — a 60-feature deep model that augments the rule tree with Orthrus pre-trained mRNA sequence embeddings and three internal XGBoost auxiliary regressors (half-life / ribosome loading / localization). No public code, weights, or precomputed predictions located at the time of writing (arXiv:2502.14547), and the published input pipeline is variant-centric (VEP-annotated stop-gain variants on a single canonical transcript per gene) rather than designed for arbitrary long-read isoform sequences.
